Abstract 27

Dropout from essential maternal health services across pregnancy, childbirth, and the 28

postnatal period remains a major barrier to improving maternal and neonatal outcomes in 29

Bangladesh. This study examined stage-specific dropout patterns along the maternal 30

continuum of care and identified factors associated with discontinuation. 31

We analysed nationally representative data from the Bangladesh Demographic and Health 32

Survey 2022 for 5,162 women with a recent live birth. Dropout from antenatal care, skilled 33

birth attendance, and postnatal care was examined using multivariable logistic regression to 34

estimate adjusted odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals, with comparisons to BDHS 35

2017–18 and assessment of regional variation. 36

Only 44% of women received four or more antenatal care visits. Of these, 33% delivered 37

with a skilled birth attendant, and among those receiving both antenatal care and skilled 38

delivery, only 15% received postnatal care within 48 hours. Overall, 57% dropped out before 39

completing adequate antenatal care, with additional dropouts between antenatal care and 40

delivery (10%) and between delivery and postnatal care (18%). Compared with 2017–18, 41

overall dropout from the maternal continuum of care more than doubled in 2022 (5.0% to 42

11.7%), driven by increased antenatal care dropout, while skilled birth attendance dropout 43

declined and postnatal care dropout increased slightly. Higher maternal education, household 44

wealth, media exposure, and women’s decision-making power were consistently associated 45

with lower odds of dropout, whereas higher birth order increased dropout risk. Substantial 46

regional variation was observed, with the highest overall dropout in Sylhet and the lowest in 47

Khulna. 48

High dropout from the maternal continuum of care in Bangladesh occurs predominantly at 49

the antenatal care stage and is shaped by socioeconomic status, birth order, women’s access 50

to information, and regional disparities. Strengthening early antenatal engagement and 51

Introduction 56

Despite global efforts, most global maternal and neonatal deaths occur in low and middle-income 57

countries (LMICs), and the majority of these countries are not on track to meet the Sustainable 58

Development Goals (SDG) targets by 2030. In LMICs alone, the maternal mortality ratio stood at 430 59

deaths per 100,000 live births in 2020 [1] and 2.3 million children died within their first month of life 60

in 2022, underscoring the urgent need to improve maternal and neonatal care in these regions [2, 3]. 61

The Continuum of Care (CoC) for maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) includes an 62

integrated service delivery  model starting from antenatal care (ANC) during pregnancy, skilled birth 63

attendance  during childbirth, and postnatal care (PNC)  in  the postpartum period [4-6]. This model 64

aims to improve maternal and newborn care, recognizing the interdependence of maternal and 65

newborn health and highlighting the need for continuation of care during the vulnerable period of 66

pregnancy, childbirth, and the immediate postnatal period [6]. ANC is the care provided by skilled 67

health-care professionals to pregnant women in order to ensure the best health conditions for both 68

mother and baby during pregnancy [7].  ANC visits can detect, address, and prevent complications 69

during pregnancy, enhancing the likelihood of receiving appropriate care during childbirth [7, 8]. 70

Skilled attendance during labor and delivery is crucial for a safe birth and essential newborn care, 71

significantly reducing the risk of mortality for both mother and baby from delivery-related 72

complications [9]. On the other hand, postnatal care (PNC), immediately after birth and continuing for 73

up to six weeks, is essential to prevent maternal death from excessive bleeding, infections, and 74

hypertensive disorder of pregnancy as well as prevent neonatal death from major causes such as 75

complications of prematurity, birth asphyxia, and sepsis [10, 11]. Therefore, successful completion of 76

the MNCH CoC can not only lower maternal and neonatal mortality and morbidities from preventable 77

The high dropout rate for MNCH CoC is a global public health challenge. Specifically, LMICs 81

observed the highest dropout rates for MNCH CoC, moving sequentially from ANC to institutional 82

delivery and from institutional delivery to PNC services [6, 12, 13]. In Africa, for example, the rates 83

range from 8% in Ghana to 31% in Nigeria [14, 15]. In India, due to substantial regional variation, 84

completion rates range from 12% to 81%, with the highest number of dropouts in the CoC observed at 85

ANC, with a loss of nearly 38% [4]. In Nepal, more than half of the pregnant women in the country 86

do not complete the CoC [16]. The dropout patterns in Africa and Southeast Asia suggest that the 87

transition from ANC to delivery care (including skilled birth attendance) is a critical point where 88

many women fall out of the CoC, emphasizing the need for strategic interventions [17]. Among the 89

socio-economic factors, poverty, distance to health facilities, limited information, poor service 90

quality, and prevailing cultural beliefs and practices have been identified as the major causes of 91

overall maternal CoC dropouts in LMICs [13, 17]. Studies also identified maternal characteristics 92

such as age at first birth, the number of children, mother’s educational attainment, household wealth, 93

place of residence, women's autonomy, and exposure to mass media, being associated with CoC. In 94

addition, this study examined regional variations in CoC dropout to capture geographic patterns of 95

maternal healthcare utilization across diverse settings, thereby providing evidence to inform policy 96

decisions and the development of targeted interventions. Understanding these geographic variations is 97

crucial, as disparities in healthcare infrastructure, service availability, and sociocultural practices 98

across regions can significantly influence women’s ability and willingness to complete the continuum 99

of maternal care. 100

Bangladesh is one of the LMICs that has made significant progress in reducing maternal and child 101

mortality over the last few decades: 322 per 100 000 live births in 2001 to 194 per 100 000 live births 102

in 2010 [18-20]. However, the country has observed a lag in the decline of maternal mortality since 103

then, as depicted by 196 maternal deaths per 100,000 in 2016 [21]. One of the major reasons for this 104

lag in decline is the high dropout from MNCH CoC. In Bangladesh, 41% of women used four and 105

above ANC, 65% had institutional delivery, and 61% of women had PNC visits [22]. The completion 106

rate of the CoC in Bangladesh is low, with only 18% of women completing all seven MNCH care 107

interventions during their reproductive lifespan [23]. The high dropout rate from the maternal CoC in 108

Bangladesh is a significant public health concern with far-reaching consequences such as missed 109

opportunities to identify and timely manage preventable causes of maternal and newborn mortality 110

and morbidities [23, 24], exacerbating  existing health inequities in maternal and newborn deaths 111

within the country [23, 25, 26] and poor maternal and newborn  health outcomes, leading  to increased 112

healthcare costs, loss of productivity, and long-term economic burdens on families and the healthcare 113

system [23, 27]. 114

This study assessed patterns and factors associated with maternal CoC dropout in Bangladesh. The 115

primary objective was to investigate the extent of dropout within and across stages of care, from 116

pregnancy to delivery and the postnatal period for mothers. The secondary objective was identifying 117

factors associated with dropouts at different continuum stages. Findings from this study inform 118

policies and design targeted interventions to improve maternal CoC in Bangladesh and globally. 119

Materials and Methods 121

Study design 122

We did a secondary analysis of the Bangladesh Demographic and Health Survey (BDHS) 2022 data 123

[28]. The national survey aimed to provide reliable demographic and health estimates for Bangladesh, 124

covering urban and rural areas of eight administrative divisions. The BDHS 2022s sampling design 125

and questionnaires can be found in the final report [28].  Briefly, the survey employed a two-stage 126

stratified sample design. The primary sampling unit (PSU) was an enumeration area (EA) with an 127

average of 120 households. A total of 675 EAs were selected, including 237 urban and 438 rural areas 128

from the 2011 Population and Housing Census [29]. In the second stage, a systematic sample of 30 129

In addition, we performed a descriptive comparison of maternal CoC dropout trends using data from 132

both BDHS 2017–18 and BDHS 2022, to assess changes over time across key care stages (ANC, 133

SBA, and PNC). 134

Study Variables 136

The outcome variable of the study is a dropout from the maternal CoC. This included four or more 137

antenatal care, delivery with a skilled birth attendance (defined as delivered by either qualified a 138

doctor, nurse, midwife, family welfare visitor (FWV), community skilled birth attendant, sub assistant 139

community medical office or community health care provider), and postnatal care (PNC) within 48 140

hours for mothers (either in a facility or at home), examining at which stages mothers might have 141

dropped out of the recommended care continuum. 142

143

This study used the definition of variables regarding dropout from the maternal care continuum from 144

previous studies [12, 13]. ANC dropout was defined as a woman who had less than four ANC visits 145

during her most recent childbirth. Skilled birth attendant (SBA) dropouts included women who had 146

four or more ANC visits but did not seek an SBA during delivery, meaning the delivery was not 147

conducted by healthcare professionals such as midwives, nurses, doctors, and/or health officers. A 148

PNC dropout was a woman who had four or more ANC visits and had SBA during delivery but did 149

not receive PNC visits within the first 48 hours of delivery. Dropouts from maternal CoC included 150

women who dropped out of ANC, SBA, and PNC. It included dropouts from the entire continuum of 151

maternal care, from pregnancy to post-delivery. 152

Our exposure variables included sociodemographic factors, reproductive and obstetric factors, and 153

women's empowerment. Sociodemographic factors included the mother's age (<20, 20-34, 35-49), 154

religion (Muslim and others), level of education (no education, primary, secondary and higher), 155

Statistical analysis 163

The analysis was performed using STATA software, version 17 and R-Studio. First, we examined the 164

socio-demographic characteristics of the study participants. Descriptive statistics were used to 165

compare dropout rates between BDHS 2017–18 and BDHS 2022. Then, we calculated the rates of 166

dropouts in each stage of CoC.  Then we estimated adjusted odd ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence 167

intervals (CIs) for the associations between dropout from each stages of the continuum of care (CoC) 168

and mother's age, religion, level of education, division, household income, area of residence, mobile 169

phone ownership, media exposure, birth order, mother's body mass index (BMI) and household 170

decision-making power using four sequential multivariable generalized linear models (GLM) with 171

binomial distribution and logit link. Each model targeted a specific stage of CoC dropout: Model I for 172

ANC dropout, Model II for SBA dropout, Model III for PNC dropout, and Model IV for dropout from 173

the overall maternal CoC. Each dropout was coded as '1' for dropout and '0' otherwise. We did not 174

include survey weights in these models. 175

We observed higher dropout rates from the maternal CoC among women aged 35 years and above 205

(20.5%) and among women without any formal education (27.1%). Regionally, the Sylhet division 206

women had a higher dropout rate (13.9%) compared to non-Muslim mothers (7.3%). CoC dropouts 210

were less frequent among women who owned mobile phones (8.7%) and those with media exposure 211

The proportion of dropouts from the continuum of maternity care 218

The flowchart illustrates the stepwise dropout rates at each stage of maternal CoC among 5,162 219

participants (Fig 1). It indicates that 44% of women received four or more ANC visits. Of those, 33% 220

had SBA during delivery. Among the women who received both four or more ANC visits and SBA, 221

only 15% received PNC. This reflects a 57% dropout rate before completing four ANC visits, a 222

further 10% dropout between ANC and SBA, and an additional 18% dropout from delivery to PNC. 223

Factors associated with the SBA dropout 262

Then we explored multivariable adjusted associations between sociodemographic, reproductive, and 263

women’s decision-making factors with dropout from SBA during delivery among women who 264

received four or more ANC (Table 2).  We found that women having higher education were less 265

likely to drop out of SBA delivery compared to women without any formal education conditional on 266

other sociodemographic, reproductive, and decision-making factors (aOR: 0.44; 95% CI 0.23-0.86). 267

We also found that women’s decision-making power reduced odd of SBA dropout by 72%. In 268

contrast, having a higher birth order increased the odds of dropout from SBA. 269

We then examined the multivariable adjusted association between sociodemographic, reproductive, 272

and women’s decision-making factors and PNC dropouts among women who have received care four 273

or more ANC and SBA during delivery (Table 2). Surprisingly, we found that women from wealthier 274

households had higher odds of PNC dropout compared to women from the poorest quintile. 275

Factors associated with dropout from the maternal CoC 279

Model IV presents multivariable adjusted associations between sociodemographic, reproductive and 280

women’s decision-making factors with dropout from CoC (ANC, SBA during delivery, and PNC). 281

We found women who completed higher education had lower odds of CoC dropout compared to 282

women without any formal education (aOR: 0.33; 95% CI: 0.16-0.68). Women from richer (0.49, 0.3- 283

0.78) and the richest (0.32, 0.17-0.6) wealth quintiles had lower odds of dropout compared to those 284

from the poorest quintile. Owning a mobile phone (aOR:0.59, 95%CI: 0.45-0.78) and having media 285

exposure (0.65, 0.49-0.87) significantly reduced the odds of dropout from CoC. Additionally, women 286

having their second birth (aOR: 2.09, 95% CI: 1.38-3.15), third birth (aOR: 2.92, 95%CI: 1.85-4.6), or 287

more show had higher odds of drop out from CoC compared to those having their first birth. 288

In Fig 3, we adjusted all model outputs to ensure the average of each model matched the overall 290

average. This makes it easier to compare across divisions while keeping the differences between 291

models intact. The heatmap reveals substantial variation in dropout rates, with the highest ANC 292

dropouts observed in Sylhet (20%) and Chattogram (18%), indicating significant gaps in early 293

maternal engagement. SBA dropouts were most pronounced in Mymensingh (≈19%) and Rangpur 294

(17%), suggesting barriers to skilled delivery services in these regions. PNC dropouts were 295

concentrated in Dhaka and Mymensingh (15%–18%), while the overall CoC dropout was highest in 296

Discussion 307

Our study provides essential insights into the patterns and determinants of dropout from maternal CoC 308

in Bangladesh. We found significant dropouts across all stages of CoC, with a high dropout from four 309

ANC visits. Among sociodemographic factors explored in this study, we found that women with 310

higher educational attainment, higher household wealth, access to a mobile phone, and media 311

exposure were less likely to drop out from the CoC compared to their counterparts. In contrast, 312

women with higher birth orders were more likely to drop out from CoC compared to women having 313

their first birth. There were regional variations in the dropout from CoC, with Sylhet and Rajshahi 314

divisions having higher ANC dropouts, and Mymensingh and Rangpur divisions having higher SBA 315

dropouts compared to the Barishal division. 316

Our results showed that more than half of the women did not receive four ANC visits during their last 317

birth, which is the first and most critical point of engagement with the health system. Although 318

coverage of  ANC by medically trained provider increased from 82% in 2017-18 to 88% in 2022 in 319

Bangladesh, only 41% of pregnant women received four or more visits in 2022 and this number 320

declined by 5% from 2017-18 [8, 22, 28]. Studies from Pakistan and Tanzania found that four or more 321

ANC visits were associated with increased continuation to SBA and PNC, highlighting the potential 322

negative implications of ANC dropout on subsequent care-seeking and maternal CoC [5, 30-32]. 323

Evidence further indicates that poor quality of ANC in LMICs, including shortages of skilled 324

providers, limited diagnostic capacity, inadequate counseling, poor communication, and lack of 325

respectful care [7], may discourage women and their families from facility delivery and PNC[25, 33]. 326

Future research should explore innovative strategies to not only improve the quality of ANC but also 327

leverage its potential as a platform to engage mothers and encourage continued care-seeking for 328

delivery and PNC services. 329

We also found that women’s higher educational attainment, access to a mobile phone, and exposure to 330

media were negatively associated with maternal CoC dropout. Evidence suggests that women's 331

education and access to mobile phones were associated with greater decision-making power and 332

higher utilization of maternal health services, including ANC and SBA [13, 25, 34]. Previous studies 333

from Bangladesh [25], Nepal [16], and Pakistan [35] have similarly found that media exposure 334

correlates with enhanced women’s decision-making autonomy and reduced maternal CoC dropout. 335

These findings underscore the potential of mobile technology to strengthen maternal CoC by 336

delivering health messages, promoting awareness of CoC benefits through digital campaigns, 337

providing SMS reminders for ANC and PNC visits, offering telemedicine services for ANC and PNC 338

in remote areas, and establishing support networks for pregnant women and new mothers[31, 36, 37]. 339

As mobile phone coverage continues to grow in Bangladesh and other LMICs, this platform offers 340

substantial promise for improving access to maternal health services, an area that warrants further 341

research[38]. 342

Our study found significant geographical and socio-economic disparities in maternal CoC dropouts in 343

Bangladesh. Notably, Sylhet and Barisal had high ANC dropout rates, while Mymensingh and 344

Rangpur showed higher dropout from SBA. We also found that women in rural areas were generally 345

more likely to discontinue CoC compared to urban women. Interestingly, ANC dropouts were higher 346

in urban areas compared to rural areas. These findings indicate the presence of context-specific 347

barriers affecting access to ANC, SBA, and PNC services, which require targeted interventions. For 348

example,  studies in urban slums of Bangladesh have identified poor service quality as one of the 349

reasons for lower ANC care seeking [39]. In contrast,  in hard-to-reach regions of Sylhet and Barisal, 350

distance to facilities, lack of transportation, and cultural or religious beliefs in conservative 351

communities appear to be major contributors to the lack of access to maternal health services, which 352

need further exploration[39, 40].  In the absence of provision of health insurance, poverty and high 353

out-of-pocket costs of care seeking may further hinder maternal care seeking[12, 23, 25]. Given this 354

context, future research should explore interventions tailored to specific local needs, such as mobile 355

clinics, outreach programs, and transportation stipends to improve geographic accessibility in remote 356

and rural areas [18, 41]. To address financial barriers to care seeking, interventions such as 357

community-based health insurance and conditional cash transfers can be examined in future studies 358

[42, 43]. Finally, engaging community leaders, including religious figures, schoolteachers, and health 359

volunteers, may help overcome sociocultural barriers that limit women’s access to maternal health 360

services and should be evaluated in future studies[14, 18]. 361

Our study has several strengths and limitations. Key strengths of our study include the use of a 362

national survey dataset, which provides comprehensive insights into maternal CoC dropouts across 363

Bangladesh. However, this study also has several limitations. Notably, we were unable to assess the 364

quality of ANC, SBA, and PNC services, which may be significant contributors to CoC dropout. 365

Additionally, we did not examine the social, cultural, and financial barriers to maternal care-seeking 366

behaviors. All these factors require further exploration in future research. 367

In conclusion, our study identified high dropouts from the maternal CoC in Bangladesh, with the 368

majority of the dropouts happening at the first point of contact of ANC. Maternal education, access to 369

mobile phones and media, and higher household wealth were associated with lower CoC dropouts. In 370

contrast, dropout rates were higher in rural areas, and we observed notable geographic disparities 371

across administrative divisions. Given the critical role of ANC in shaping subsequent care-seeking 372

behaviors and the promise of mHealth interventions, both should be explored as platforms for 373

generating demand and improving continued engagement with maternal health services. Additionally, 374

future research should explore contextual barriers at each stage of ANC, SBA, and PNC, including 375

issues related to service quality, geographic accessibility, and socio-cultural and economic factors, 376

and develop and evaluate targeted interventions to address these challenges. 377
